title: Hiroshi Okuda, Former Toyota CEO, Dies at 93
paragraphs: Hiroshi Okuda, the former Toyota chief who helped turn the company into one of the world's leading carmakers, has died at the age of 93.
Toyota announced his death in August. The date and cause of his death were not immediately made public, and his family is handling the funeral arrangements.

Okuda was born in central Japan, the region where Toyota has its headquarters, and graduated from Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo in 1955 with a business degree. He went on to spend 45 years at Toyota. Unusually, he was not a member of the Toyoda family, which founded the company and has provided most of its leaders. In 1995, he became the first person from outside the family to become Toyota's president in 28 years. He then served as chairman until 2006.

Okuda is perhaps best remembered for leading the development of the Prius. Released in 1997, the gas-electric hybrid car was groundbreaking at the time and later became a symbol of the car industry's move toward greener driving. He also helped build Toyota's reputation for fuel efficiency.

Under Okuda's leadership, Toyota expanded rapidly around the world, setting up factories in the United States and Europe. His efforts helped lay the foundation for Toyota's rise to become the world's largest automaker.

His influence extended beyond Toyota. He served as chairman of Keidanren, Japan's most powerful business organization, and headed other major groups, including the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association. He was also known for promoting younger executives, which was uncommon in Japanese companies at the time.
Okuda was described as outspoken and quick to laugh, and he held a black belt in judo. He often stressed that the car industry was global and connected, frequently using the word "harmony."
In 2005, he told reporters that a company must change when things are going well, adding that there is no point in trying to change after things start going badly.
